job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Victor Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior financial controller at a freight company at the port of Valencia, with a business degree from the university there. I check freight invoices, build monthly reports and answer to our finance director, Elena. I share a flat with my cousin Pablo, who works in the port office. On Saturdays I help in my parents' hardware store, and on Sundays I go to mass with my grandmother and have lunch with the whole family. I use AI tools every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say fine, more of the same. To my family I'd say I always thought it was partly hype. Online I'd post about the store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I'm a little let down. I use AI every day to check freight invoices and build reports, and I wanted it to go further so I could help my father's store. But even a small tool saves me a lot of time, so I'll keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at work and use weekends to put the store's stock on a simple system. My father still writes orders on paper. I'd save six hundred a month and put a share into the store when it needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'm busy, I like it, and I have a family business to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the store.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ferretería Diaz, on Calle Sagunto. My father Rafael has run it for thirty years. He knows every customer by name and which screw they want. My mother Carmen does the till. They've never thought about computers, and I want to change that without making them feel old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you do that without upsetting them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. I'd start with something that saves my mother's time, like a printout of what to reorder every Monday. If she likes it, my father will follow. In our family, you earn trust by being useful first.

say: I'd tell colleagues it's **more of the same**, and my family I always thought it was partly hype.
I'd post about the family store online.
think: I'm a little let down; I hoped AI would go further so I could help the **store**.
Even a small tool saves me a lot of time at work.
do: Use weekends to put the store's **stock** on a simple system.
Save about **£600 a month** and put some into the store.
Keep using AI daily at work.
feel: **Calm**; I'm busy, I like it and have a family business as backup.
S0.quote: In our family, you earn trust by being useful first.
fieldNote: Wants to modernise his parents' shop **without making them** feel old.
The store is his **safety net** and his project.
Uses AI daily and treats a plateau as a **missed chance**.

steps.text: Put the store's stock on a simple system on weekends
Put part of my savings into the store when it needs it
Keep using AI daily to check freight invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. It's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's be first to use the tools in the controlling team. To my family I'd say jobs change but families stay. Online I'd share what I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job, mostly checking and reporting, gets reshaped fast. The firm's controlling team of eight could become five. I want to be one of the ones who runs the tools, and I'm already halfway there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to lead the move of our month-end reporting onto the tools. I'd put the store's ordering on the same kind of system. And I'd study for a master's in data and finance in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A little excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin Pablo, who works in the port office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Pablo to learn the basics now and not wait for the firm to teach him. He's stubborn and says the port office never changes. I'd bet him a paella that it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the store goes the other way. If bigger chains use AI to cut prices, small stores can't keep up. My father's customers are loyal, but loyalty has a price limit. I'd rather help him win on service than fight on price.

say: I'd say let's be **first to use** the tools in the controlling team.
I'd tell my family that jobs change but families stay.
think: My team of eight could become five, and I want to be one of those who **runs the tools**.
do: Offer to lead the **month-end reporting** move onto the tools.
Put the store's **ordering** on a similar system.
Study a master's in data and finance in the evenings.
S1.quote: My father's customers are loyal, but loyalty has a price limit.
fieldNote: Treats adoption as a **career lever** and takes the lead on it.
His fear sits with the **store**, not his own job.
Warns his cousin to learn now, not wait for the firm.

steps.text: Offer to lead the month-end reporting move onto the tools

Start a master's in data and finance in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a plan this month about who runs what. To my family I'd say we must stay together and everyone saves. Online I'd say little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I could lose my job within two years, and the store faces the same wave. I use the tools daily, which helps, but when the machine does the controller's work I'm just a user of the thing that replaces me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save about nine hundred a month and move back home for a while to cut rent. I'd rebuild the store as a small modern shop: online orders, home delivery and a stock system. And I'd talk to our parish about helping neighbours who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be working all hours, which is how I handle fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years not give you time for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not enough time to make the store modern and also pay for it. Rebuilding takes eighteen months and some money. If I start now, I'd just about make it. If I wait to see what happens, I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would resist, then come round. He'd say the store has survived worse, and then ask me what a stock system is. My mother would be the first to say yes. I'd have to bring them along gently.

say: I'd say we need a **plan this month** about who runs what.
I'd tell my family we must stay together and everyone saves.
think: I could lose my job in two years, and the **store** faces the same wave.
Using the tools daily means I use the thing that replaces me.
do: Save about **£900 a month** and move back home to cut rent.
Rebuild the store with **online orders** and home delivery.
Talk to our parish about helping neighbours who lose work.
feel: **Anxious**; I'd work all hours, which is how I handle fear.
S2.quote: If I start now, I'd just about make it. If I wait to see what happens, I wouldn't.
fieldNote: Fear turns to **work**, not freeze: rebuild the store while he can.
Moving home shows **family** as the real cushion.
Brings the **parish** into the plan, a traditional-minded reflex.

steps.text: Move back to my parents' flat to cut rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough to rebuild the team around people who run the tools. To my family I'd say start building something that lasts. Online I'd say nothing, just work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be okay. I'd have the store, my skills and a head start. I'd be one of the people who adapted early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to modernise the store with online ordering and home delivery. I'd study the evening master's. I'd set up a small advisory service for other family shops in the neighbourhood, using AI to do their books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a lot, but it's a good lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. I have time to start something and keep a salary while it grows. In two years I'd be gambling. In five, I'm investing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the store doesn't make it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we sell the shop front and my parents retire on that, with a bit from me. I'd still have the advisory work and my degree. Family comes first, the shop second.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **rebuild the team** around people who run the tools.
I'd tell family to build something that lasts.
think: I'd be okay, with the **store**, my skills and a head start.
I'd be among those who adapted early.
do: Spend two years **modernising the store** with online orders and delivery.
Offer AI-based bookkeeping to other family shops.
feel: **Calm**; it's a lot, but a good lot.
S3.quote: In two years I'd be gambling. In five, I'm investing.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **keep a salary** while the store and advice work grow.
Puts **family before shop**, ready to sell the shop front for his parents.
Builds a second business out of **AI-based bookkeeping**.

steps.text: Add online ordering and home delivery to the store
Study the evening master's in data and finance
Offer AI-based bookkeeping to other family shops
Put part of my savings into the store's upgrade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a long runway and we can do this well. To my family I'd say start saving for the next generation. Online I'd post about the store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good. By thirty-two I could run the store with two employees, or have my own advisory firm, and have a family. Ten years is enough for all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the store step by step, finish a master's, and buy a flat in Valencia. I'd marry, if I've met the right person, and keep going to mass with my grandmother on Sundays. I'd also invest in index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and ambitious. Ten years is a long time to be afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn to read people, to work with their hands as well as screens, and to keep family close. I'd teach them that a good name is worth more than any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people with no family business or savings are left with nothing. I believe in work and in markets, but if a whole generation has no way in, markets don't work. Parishes and neighbours can help, but it needs more than that.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway** and we can do this well.
I'd tell family to start saving for the next generation.
think: I'd feel good; by thirty-two I could run the store or have my own **advisory firm**.
Ten years is enough for work, a family and a flat.
do: Build the store **step by step** and finish a master's.
Buy a **flat in Valencia** and invest in index funds.
Keep going to mass with my grandmother on Sundays.
feel: **Calm and ambitious**; ten years is a long time to be afraid.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time to be afraid.
fieldNote: Plans a **whole life**: store, firm, flat, family, mass on Sundays.
His concern is people with **no way in**, which he says markets alone won't fix.
Defines value as **a good name**, not skills alone.

steps.text: Finish a master's in data and finance
Buy a flat in Valencia and plan a family
Save for the store's next upgrade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years leaves me only just enough time to rebuild the store, and my job could go at the same moment. Cheap loans for small family shops to modernise would help, and training that pays people while they learn. And firms and government telling us the truth early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That I'm lucky to have a family business to fall back on, and most people don't. I'd like to help them with work, not charity. A good name is worth more than any machine.

headlineQuote: A good name is worth more than any machine.
portrait: Victor is a **22-year-old junior controller** in Valencia, top of his class, with no debt and a family store behind him.
He uses AI **every day**, and wants to bring his father's hardware shop into the modern world.
He is traditional on **faith, family and community**, and favours work and markets over handouts.
He stays calm in most pictures but turns **anxious at 2028**, when job and store are both at risk.
His answer to fear is **hard work**: rebuild the store, save, and bring his parents along.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because it leaves just enough time to rebuild the store.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small family shops to modernise.
**Paid training** and early honesty from firms and government.
